studies.title: Thus He Inspires You
studies.meaning: The surah opens with two sets of disconnected letters and then a sentence that does not explain them. What it explains instead is the process the reader is inside: this is how He inspires you, and how He inspired those before you. Revelation is presented as ongoing practice rather than a new event. Four names follow across two lines, two of power and wisdom, two of height and greatness, and between them sits a statement of ownership that leaves nothing outside.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah addressed to a small community whose claim to a revelation was being ridiculed by people who controlled the city. Opening by placing this revelation in a line with earlier ones answers that ridicule without argument. Commentators report no particular occasion for these lines. The surah takes its name from a single word much later in it, about deciding matters by consultation.

keyTerms.note: The verb is in the present tense, which in Arabic covers action still going on. Revelation is described as something happening rather than as a completed deposit handed over once.
From the root for height. Classical readers take it as elevation in rank and worth rather than in place, since the previous line has just said everything is already His.
From a root that also gives the words for judgement and for the bit that steers an animal. Wisdom here carries restraint and direction, not just knowledge of how things work.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca was a town of specialists in speech. Poets, orators and soothsayers all claimed some access to words that came from elsewhere, and audiences were practised at telling one kind from another. A recitation that opened with detached letters and refused to explain them would have registered immediately as unlike all three. Its first listeners knew the categories well enough to notice that this did not fit them.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only surah in the Quran whose opening letters are split across two separate ayat, one set and then another. It is also one of seven consecutive surahs, from the fortieth to the forty-sixth, that all begin with the same two letters, so this surah carries the group's shared opening and one additional set found nowhere else.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage grounds the Prophet's experience in a pattern rather than in a singular event, which changes what is being claimed. If the same verb describes what happened to those before him, then the question for a listener is not whether such a thing can occur but whether it has occurred again. And the unexplained letters make a point of their own: a revelation that begins with something withheld is not offering itself as fully transparent.

crossReferences.why: Lists the earlier recipients this line gestures at, naming prophets from Noah onwards as inspired in the same way.
Describes the same inspiration from the receiving end, as something taught rather than composed.
Addresses passages whose meaning is not made plain, and describes two ways of responding to what is withheld.

studies.applyIt: Read the first two lines of this surah aloud and let yourself not understand them. Do not look up an explanation today. Sit with the fact that the text opens by handing you something you cannot use, and notice how quickly you want that resolved. The discomfort is worth more than the answer for one sitting.

studies.title: The Angels Ask For Us
studies.meaning: The heavens are described as nearly splitting from above, and then the sentence moves without pause to what the angels are doing. They praise, and they ask forgiveness for whoever is on earth. Commentators connect the strain in the first clause to the claims being made about God below, and read the angels' asking as the counterweight. The next line then tells the Prophet what is not his: the people who take other protectors are God's business, and he is not their overseer.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, early in a surah addressed to a Prophet whose position in the city was worsening and who had begun to feel responsible for people refusing him. Commentators read the relief offered here as specific to that pressure. No occasion is reported for the ayat. The reference to those taking other masters fits a setting where the sanctuary itself housed the alternatives.

keyTerms.note: An intensive verb for cracking open along a seam. The same form appears in only one other place, describing the heavens straining at a claim made about God having a child.
A verb of asking on behalf of another. The object here is everyone on earth without qualification, which classical commentators noted as broader than the wording used in some parallel passages.
A word for an agent entrusted with someone else's affairs and answerable for them. Denying the role to the Prophet removes a burden rather than a privilege.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Intercession was a working part of Arabian life. A man in trouble found someone with standing to speak for him, and much of tribal politics ran on who would carry whose case. The idols at the sanctuary were valued largely for this: they were thought to put in a word. Against that background, being told that angels ask forgiveness for everyone on earth rearranged who the effective advocates were.
studies.didYouKnow: The intensive verb for the heavens nearly splitting occurs twice in the Quran and nowhere else. Its other appearance is in a surah where the strain is caused by the claim that the Merciful has taken a child. Here the same near-rupture is set beside angels asking forgiveness for everyone below, so the identical image serves opposite ends.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts a cosmic reaction and a routine act of intercession in the same sentence, which keeps the scale of the offence and the scale of the mercy in view together. It also draws a boundary around a messenger's responsibility. He delivers; he does not own the outcome. That distinction protects both the Prophet and anyone who has ever felt accountable for another person's belief.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who carry the Throne asking forgiveness for the believers, a narrower version of the same intercession.
Supplies the other occurrence of the heavens nearly splitting, and names the claim that causes it.
States the same limit on the Prophet's role, that he is a reminder and not a controller over people.

studies.applyIt: Name one person whose choices you have been quietly carrying: a sibling, a friend who has drifted, someone you keep arguing with in your head. Say for them the kind of thing the angels are described as saying, once, and then deliberately put the outcome down. The second half of that is the harder half and the one this passage is about.

studies.title: The Mother Of Cities
studies.meaning: The revelation is described by its language and by its first audience: an Arabic recitation, sent so that you may warn the mother of cities and those around it. Commentators identify the mother of cities as Mecca and read the phrase as naming a centre from which something spreads. The second half names what the warning is about. Not a raid or a famine, but a day of gathering that carries no doubt, at the end of which the assembly divides in two and the sentence simply stops there.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience is the town itself and the settlements and tribes in its orbit, which is how the earliest reach of the message is described elsewhere too. Commentators note that the Quran being in Arabic is raised repeatedly in this period as an argument, since the objection that it was unclear could not be made against speech in the hearers' own tongue. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A phrase for a place other places grow around and depend on. Arabic uses mother for the origin or main body of a thing, so the image is of a source rather than a capital.
From the ordinary verb for collecting people together. It names the Day by its most social feature, everyone in one place, before saying anything at all about judgement.
A word for a section separated off from a larger body, used twice here. It keeps the division collective rather than individual, which is unusual in descriptions of that Day.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca sat where trade routes met and drew its importance from the sanctuary and the markets around it. Tribes camped in its orbit, pilgrims came in season, and news travelled outward with the caravans that left for Syria and Yemen. Calling it the mother of settlements described a real dependency: what was said in Mecca was carried to places that had never sent anyone there.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for the mother of settlements occurs twice in the Quran, and the other instance uses almost the same wording about warning it and whoever is around it. The name for the Day of Gathering used here occurs only in this ayah, though a related phrase appears once elsewhere. The surah names the Day by its assembly rather than by its reckoning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage ties a universal warning to a specific address. The message goes out in one language, from one town, to people who could hear it without translation, and the Day it warns of belongs to everyone. Holding both together is the Quran's usual position: revelation arrives in a particular place and speech, and what it announces is not particular at all. The final division is stated without any softening.

crossReferences.why: Uses nearly the identical phrase about warning the mother of settlements and those around it, describing another Book.
Names the same Day of Gathering with a related phrase, and describes what happens to those who believe.
Gives the same reason for the recitation being in Arabic, that its hearers might understand it.

studies.applyIt: Read a passage today in a translation you do not usually use, alongside your normal one. Notice a place where the two disagree about a word. This ayah makes a point of the message arriving in a language its first hearers already had. Yours arrives through someone's choices, and it is worth seeing where those choices sit.

studies.title: He Could Have Made One Community
studies.meaning: The line concedes something before anyone asks. Uniformity was available and was not chosen. Commentators take this as an answer to the question that follows any failed argument: if the truth is clear, why is anyone still outside it. The reply does not explain the reason; it states that the arrangement is deliberate. Then admission into mercy is described as an act of will rather than an entitlement, and the last clause says what the wrongdoers lack, naming two roles at once, a protector and a helper.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a stretch of the surah dealing with the Prophet's responsibility for a city that would not respond. The preceding line has already told him he is not their overseer, and this one supplies the reason: the diversity of belief in front of him is not a failure of the message. Commentators report no occasion. The same statement recurs across several Meccan surahs in nearly identical wording.

keyTerms.note: The word covers a people, a generation and a way of life together. Making them one would mean not merely agreement but a single shape of living, which is what the sentence says was not done.
The one who stands close enough to act for you. In Arabian society this was a legal position with obligations attached, not a feeling of goodwill toward someone.
One who comes to your aid at the moment of need. Pairing it with the previous word covers both standing relationship and emergency assistance, so the denial leaves nothing open.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man alone in Arabia was in danger. Protection came from a patron with standing and from allies who would answer a call, and losing both was a practical catastrophe rather than a metaphor. Men who converted in Mecca sometimes found exactly this happening to them as their families withdrew cover. The two words denied at the end of this ayah named the two things everybody had and everybody needed.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for one single community occurs nine times in the Quran. In several of those places it appears in exactly this construction, saying that God could have made people one and did not, and in others it describes humanity as having once been one before differing. The same two words carry both the road not taken and the starting point departed from.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats disagreement as permitted rather than accidental, which removes a particular kind of anxiety without offering an explanation. It also separates being brought into mercy from being able to claim it. And by naming what the wrongdoers lack rather than what they will suffer, the ayah defines loss as being without anyone, which is a different and more recognisable thing than punishment.

crossReferences.why: States the same thing and adds that they will not cease to differ, making the situation permanent rather than temporary.
Repeats the identical concession and follows it with the promise that everyone will be asked about what they did.
Gives the reason more fully, that the different ways are a test in doing good rather than a defect.

studies.applyIt: Think of one person whose refusal to see something obvious has been bothering you for months. Try saying, once, that their being outside your agreement is not a problem you were assigned. You may still talk to them tomorrow. But notice how much of the weight came from believing the gap was yours to close.

studies.title: Or Have They Taken Protectors
studies.meaning: A question that is really an objection: have they gone and taken patrons other than Him. The answer does not argue against the alternatives. It states the position and moves on, then adds two capacities as evidence rather than as praise. He gives life to the dead, and He has power over everything. Commentators note the choice of proof: reviving the dead is the one thing no patron in Arabia could offer, which quietly settles what a protector is worth by naming the limit of every other one.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just told the Prophet that those who take other masters are not his responsibility, and this line turns from him to them. Patronage in Mecca was the framework everything ran on, and the objects at the sanctuary were understood partly in those terms. No occasion is reported for the ayah; commentators read it as part of the surah's opening argument about who is actually in charge.

keyTerms.note: A particle introducing an alternative that the speaker finds unlikely. Arabic uses it to raise a possibility in order to dismiss it, so the question arrives already carrying its own answer.
The same word used in the plural a clause earlier, now singular and definite. The sentence does not deny that people have patrons; it says only one of them holds the title properly.
Placed as proof rather than as doctrine. Reviving is offered here as the test a protector must pass, and it is the point at which every human patron stops being useful.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Patronage was the load-bearing structure of Meccan life. A weaker clan attached itself to a stronger one, freed slaves stayed tied to the household that released them, and traders travelled under the protection of names that meant something on the road. Everyone could say who their patron was. Asking whether people had taken protectors was not an abstract question; it was asking them to name someone.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses the word for protector both in the plural for what people take up and in the singular for God, often within a line or two of each other, as here. The same term covers the freed slave's tie to a household, the ally's obligation in war, and the relationship this surah is describing, so the vocabulary of belonging is doing all three jobs at once.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not deny that people need patrons; it competes for the position. That is a different move from dismissing the impulse, and it takes seriously why anyone attaches themselves to a power in the first place. The evidence offered is also chosen carefully. Ability over everything is a claim about scope, but reviving the dead is a claim about the one situation in which every other protection has already failed.

crossReferences.why: Names God as the protector of those who believe and describes what that protection actually does for them.
Compares taking protectors besides God to a spider's house, the frailest of dwellings, if they only knew.
Uses the reviving of dead earth as evidence for the same capacity being offered here as proof.

studies.applyIt: Write down, honestly, the three things you would contact first if something went badly wrong tonight. A person, an account, an institution. Do not judge the list. Just look at where it stops, and notice that this ayah picks its evidence at exactly the point where every entry on your list runs out.

studies.title: Whatever You Differ About
studies.meaning: A general principle and then a personal sentence, and the shift between them is the point. Any matter you disagree about goes back to God for decision; the scope is unrestricted. Then the voice changes and becomes first person. Such is God, my Lord, in Him I have put my trust, and to Him I turn. Commentators read the second half as the speech the Prophet is given to say, so a rule about arbitration is immediately shown being lived by someone rather than merely stated.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah preoccupied with division: between the Prophet and his city, and among the communities given scripture before. The principle here is stated before any of that is described in detail. Commentators report no occasion. The first-person declaration that follows belongs to a pattern in Meccan surahs where the Prophet is instructed to state his own position rather than to argue with anyone.

keyTerms.note: The noun from the verb to decide between parties. The suffix refers back to the disputed matter itself, so what is handed over is the case rather than the people arguing over it.
From the same root as the word for an agent entrusted with your affairs. It means appointing someone to act for you, which is a decision made once rather than a feeling maintained.
A verb of returning repeatedly to a place, used for a person who keeps coming back after going off. It carries habit, so the turning is not described as a single dramatic moment.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Disputes in Arabia went to arbitration. Two parties agreed on a judge, often a man from a neutral clan known for fairness, and both bound themselves in advance to accept what he said. Choosing the arbitrator was half the quarrel, and a bad choice was worse than none. The vocabulary of this ayah is that vocabulary, addressed to people who knew exactly what agreeing on a judge cost.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for turning back used at the end of this ayah reappears three lines later, where God is said to guide to Himself whoever turns to Him in this way. The surah puts the human movement and the divine response into the same word within a few ayat, so the answer to the turning is described using the turning's own vocabulary.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage does not promise that disagreements will be resolved now. It says where the decision sits, which is a claim about jurisdiction rather than about timing. That distinction lets a person hold a position without needing to win, since the case has already been filed elsewhere. And the personal declaration attached to it shows that the doctrine is only usable in the first person; stated about someone else it does nothing at all.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction for a community, referring disputed matters back to God and His Messenger.
Puts the same referral in a supplication, asking God to judge between servants in what they differed over.
Pairs the same two verbs, trusting and turning back, in the mouth of a prophet facing a town that refused him.

studies.applyIt: Take one argument you are currently losing and have kept alive in your head. Write the sentence from this ayah at the top of a page, then write the argument underneath in three lines. Leave it there for a week without adding to it. The point is not to give up your position but to stop carrying the verdict.

studies.title: There Is Nothing Like Him
studies.meaning: Two halves that look mismatched are doing one job. The first describes making and increase: mates from among yourselves, pairs among the animals, and a verb meaning to scatter seed, which is how the multiplying is pictured. Then the sentence turns and denies likeness altogether. The commentators discuss the doubled construction in the Arabic, which places two words for resemblance side by side, and generally read the repetition as strengthening the denial. Two names follow at once, and they keep the denial from producing distance.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah has just said that God could have made people a single community and did not, and that whatever people differ about returns to Him for judgement. This ayah states the ground underneath all of that. In Mecca the objects of devotion were imagined on a human scale, with lineages, preferences and rivalries, so a sentence removing likeness entirely cut against the way divinity was ordinarily pictured.

keyTerms.note: A farming verb for broadcasting seed by hand across a field. Applied to human increase, it counts people the way a grower counts a crop, which is why it follows the mention of pairs.
Two words for resemblance placed together, one meaning like and one meaning the likeness of. Grammarians have debated the construction for centuries and generally treat the doubling as emphasis.

An intensive form, not a description of an organ. Placed immediately after likeness is denied, it prevents the denial from being read as remoteness, since hearing implies a listener close enough to be addressed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Increase was how wealth was counted. Seed went out by hand across a field and was measured at harvest; animals were paired deliberately and the year's lambs and calves were tallied against the last. A household's future was the size of that number. The verb this ayah uses for human multiplying is the one a farmer used, which places people inside the same accounting as the flocks.
studies.didYouKnow: The clause denying likeness contains two separate words for resemblance in a row, which by ordinary grammar would produce the odd sense of nothing being like His likeness. Classical grammarians have written on the construction at length and generally hold that the doubling intensifies rather than qualifies, so the denial is stronger and not weaker for it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The denial sits in the middle of the description rather than at its end, and so governs what stands on both sides of it. Making and pairing are described, likeness is refused, hearing and seeing are affirmed. The order is doing the work: the refusal stops the earlier images from being assembled into a portrait, and the two names stop the refusal from producing a God too abstract to address.

crossReferences.why: Closes the shortest statement of the same point with a denial of anything comparable to Him.
Puts the limit in terms of sight, vision unable to grasp Him while He grasps vision entirely.
Names the practice this ayah rules out, coining comparisons for God out of what is at hand.

studies.applyIt: Notice the picture you are using the next time you address God: a direction, a height, a face, a presence with a shape. Everyone has one. Set it down for the length of a single prayer and speak anyway. This ayah does not offer a better picture. It removes the category and then says He hears you.

studies.title: The Keys Of The Heavens
studies.meaning: One image and one mechanism. The keys of the heavens and the earth are His, and then the mechanism is described in two directions at once: He spreads provision wide for whom He wills, and He narrows it. Commentators are careful with the second verb, which means to measure out rather than to withhold, so the narrowing is portioning and not refusal. The closing clause supplies what the whole sentence rests on. He knows everything, which is what makes a measured portion different from an arbitrary one.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a run of ayat establishing ownership and control before the surah turns to its main argument about religion and division. Provision was a live subject for a community losing trade and social support in the city. Commentators report no occasion. The pairing of spreading and measuring recurs in several Meccan surahs, always attached to a statement about knowledge.

keyTerms.note: A plural for keys or for what fastens and unfastens. It appears in only one other place in the Quran, and in both it is followed immediately by a statement about what is done with them.
The verb for laying something flat and open, used of spreading a cloth or an arm. It pictures provision as extended surface rather than as quantity, so more means further reach.
From the root for measure and capacity, the same root behind the word for divine determining. It means fixing an exact amount, which is why commentators resist reading it simply as withholding.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Grain and dates were measured, not weighed, and the measure itself was a physical object people trusted or argued about. A household's year was a series of portions: this much per person, this much held back for seed, this much owed. Nobody had a continuous supply. The verb this ayah uses for narrowing is the ordinary language of that arithmetic, not the language of a door being shut.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for keys used here occurs twice in the whole Quran, both times in the same phrase about the heavens and the earth, and both times in Meccan surahs that then say something different about what follows. Here it leads to provision being portioned out; in the other place it leads straight to a statement about those who reject the signs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes both abundance and constraint as active decisions by the same one, which removes the idea that hardship is a gap in supervision. Attaching knowledge at the end is what keeps this from being a doctrine of raw power. A portion measured by someone who knows everything about the recipient is a different object from a portion that simply happened to arrive, even when the amount is identical.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same pair of verbs about provision and adds that He is aware and seeing of His servants.
Uses the same spreading and measuring, attaching it to those He wills among His servants.
Gives the other occurrence of the keys of the heavens and the earth, in nearly identical wording.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing you currently have less of than you want: money, time, health, company. Instead of asking why, ask what the exact amount is. Write the number or the shape of it down. The verb in this ayah is about measuring, and a measured shortage behaves differently in the mind from a vague one.

studies.title: The Same Road Laid Out
studies.meaning: A single religion is traced through five names, with the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) placed inside the list rather than at its end. What was enjoined on Noah, what was inspired here, what was enjoined on Abraham, Moses and Jesus is described as one thing, and then summarised in two commands: hold the religion upright and do not split over it. Commentators read the common content as the core, not the particulars of practice. The ayah then concedes how heavy this sounds to those it is addressed to.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Naming Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus together answered an audience that knew of scriptural communities and regarded them as separate peoples with separate gods and books. The Quran's claim of a single line running through all of them was unfamiliar and, as the ayah says plainly, unwelcome. Commentators report no specific occasion. The word for laying down a way here is the root behind later terms for revealed law.

keyTerms.note: The verb occurs only here in the Quran. Its root names the path down a bank to water, so a way opened toward what people need rather than a set of rules imposed.
The verb for standing something up and keeping it standing, used of prayer and of scales. It asks for maintenance rather than for founding, which assumes the thing already exists.

keyTerms.gloss: He selects, He gathers to Himself
keyTerms.note: A verb for collecting something choice out of a larger quantity, used of picking fruit. It occurs twice in the Quran, and both times the selecting is done by God.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Quraysh traced their standing to Abraham and the sanctuary he was said to have raised, and they knew the names of Noah and Moses from traders and from the scriptural communities on their routes. What they did not have was a way of connecting those figures into one line. Their own religious world was made of separate patrons for separate needs, which is exactly the arrangement this ayah cuts against.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for laying open a way occurs only in this ayah in the entire Quran, though two related nouns from the same root appear elsewhere. The root's basic meaning is the sloped path leading down to a watering place, so the vocabulary later used for revealed law begins as a word about access to water in a dry country.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes unity a matter of continuity rather than of agreement reached later. If the same thing was enjoined across that span, then division is a departure from something older than any of the parties dividing. It also puts the instruction in two halves that need each other. Holding a religion upright without avoiding division produces rigidity; avoiding division without holding anything upright produces nothing at all.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same instruction against splitting, using the image of holding fast to a rope together.
States that this community of yours is one community, addressed after a long list of the same prophets.
Uses a noun from the same root for the way laid out, telling the Prophet to follow it and not the desires of others.

studies.applyIt: Pick one practice you keep because it is what your family or community does, and find out what a person in a very different setting does for the same purpose. Not to change yours. Just to locate which part of it is the thing itself and which part is the shape your particular place gave it.

studies.title: They Split After The Knowledge Came
studies.meaning: The sequence is the argument. Division did not come from ignorance, and it did not come first; it came after knowledge arrived, and the cause named is rivalry among themselves. Commentators stress that the word covers envy and overreach rather than honest misunderstanding, which changes what kind of problem division is. A prior decision from the Lord, set to a named term, is the only reason the matter has not already been closed. The line ends with the heirs of the Book left in unsettling doubt.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The previous ayah has just traced one religion through Noah, Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and this one explains what happened to it. Commentators read the heirs of the Book as later generations who received scripture from their predecessors without the circumstances that produced it. No occasion is reported. The setting is a city where the Prophet's own community was small enough for division to be an urgent risk.

keyTerms.note: A noun for wanting more than one's share and pressing past a limit. Naming it as the cause makes division a moral event rather than an intellectual one, which is the ayah's main claim.
A fixed period with an appointed end. The phrase recurs across the Quran for spans that are set in advance, so the delay described here is scheduled rather than merely unexplained.
A passive verb from the vocabulary of estates. Scripture arrives to them the way property does, without their having been present for the events that produced it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Inheritance disputes were among the most bitter quarrels in Arabian society, and a division of property could set cousins against each other for a generation. Everyone understood that receiving something you did not earn changes your relationship to it. Describing a community as having inherited a book placed scripture inside that familiar and complicated experience, where the thing received is genuinely yours and genuinely not.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for a term already named occurs sixteen times in the Quran in this exact form. It covers the due date of a written debt, the span appointed for the heavens and the earth, and here the delay before a communal dispute is settled. The same two words carry a loan's deadline and the end of a world.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage identifies knowledge as the trigger for division rather than its cure, which is an uncomfortable claim and a realistic one. Groups that share a text have more to fight over, not less. Naming rivalry as the cause also refuses to let disputants describe themselves as simply following the evidence. And the delay before judgement is presented as mercy in the form of time, which is the only form it can take here.

crossReferences.why: Says those given the Book divided only after the clear evidence reached them, in almost the same order.
Traces the same movement from one community to division after the Book came, naming rivalry as the cause.
Repeats the pattern for a people given clear commands who differed out of rivalry once knowledge had come.

studies.applyIt: Recall a falling-out you have watched inside a community you belong to. Ask what each side actually wanted that was not part of the stated disagreement: standing, credit, a hearing. You do not need to raise it with anyone. Naming it once for yourself is what this ayah does, and it makes the next such argument easier to see early.

studies.title: We Have Our Deeds And You Have Yours
studies.meaning: The Prophet is told to keep calling, to stay straight, and not to take his direction from what others want. Then he is given words to say, and the words are unusually generous. I believe in whatever Book God sent down. God is our Lord and your Lord. Our deeds are ours and yours are yours. No argument between us. Commentators read the last phrase as declining a quarrel rather than conceding a point, and note that the sentence ends by handing the whole disagreement to a future gathering.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to a Prophet who was under pressure to trim his message to what his audience would accept. The declaration he is given acknowledges earlier scripture in general terms, which fits an audience that included people aware of Jewish and Christian communities. Commentators report no specific occasion. The instruction to remain upright appears in similar wording at several points in this period.

keyTerms.note: A verb for holding a straight line, used of a road and of a standing pillar. It asks for direction maintained over time rather than for a single act of resolve.
The plural of a word whose root means falling. It names wanting that pulls downward and shifts, which is why it is set against the straight line in the previous clause.
A word for the case one party presses against another. Denying that there is any between us refuses the contest itself, not the possibility that one side is right.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public argument was entertainment and politics at once. Men gathered to hear a case pressed, judged the performance, and remembered who had been left without an answer. Refusing to enter such a contest was a visible act with a cost, easily read as weakness. What this ayah gives the Prophet to say would have sounded, in that setting, like a man declining a fight he was expected to want.
studies.didYouKnow: The word given here for the argument that is refused is the same word the very next ayah applies to those who dispute about God, saying their case has no footing. Two consecutive ayat use it, once for a quarrel declined and once for a quarrel pressed and found empty, setting the two responses directly beside each other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates conviction from combativeness, which is harder than it sounds because the two usually travel together. The speaker states his belief without qualification and declines the contest in the same breath. It also relocates the settlement: God will bring us together. That makes coexistence now possible without either side pretending the difference does not matter, since the difference is being kept rather than dissolved.

crossReferences.why: Ends a whole surah with the same separation of ways, stated even more briefly and without any argument attached.
Gives the same instruction to stand straight as commanded, with a warning against overstepping in the process.
Tells believers how to speak with people of earlier scripture, using nearly the same phrase about one God for both.

studies.applyIt: In your next disagreement about something that matters, say your own position once, clearly, and then say nothing further to win it. Notice the pull to add one more line. That pull is the thing this ayah is addressing, and it usually has more to do with the audience than with the truth of what you said.

studies.title: An Argument With No Footing
studies.meaning: The people described are not those who never heard. They are arguing about God after His call has already been answered, which commentators read either as after the message was accepted by others or after they themselves had responded once. Their case is described with a word for a foot slipping on wet ground: it has no purchase. Three consequences follow in a compressed line, the void argument, anger, and a severe punishment, and nothing is said about the content of what they were arguing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Opposition in the city hardened as the message gained a hearing, and some of those disputing had watched people they knew respond to it. Commentators note that the ayah addresses argument that begins after a matter has already moved, rather than initial objection. No specific occasion is reported. The surah has just given the Prophet words that decline a quarrel, and this line describes the quarrel he is declining.

keyTerms.gloss: they dispute, they press a case
keyTerms.note: A reciprocal form, so both sides are pushing. The verb belongs to formal argument between parties rather than to private doubt, which is why a public setting is assumed.
From a root for a foot sliding on slick ground. The word occurs only here, and it describes an argument that cannot stand rather than one that has been refuted.
Given without the definite article, so a portion of anger rather than the whole of it. Arabic uses the indefinite here to weigh rather than to soften, leaving the quantity unstated.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan disputes were settled in the open, and the loser lost standing as well as the point. A man who kept arguing after the room had moved on was a recognisable figure, and there were poems mocking him. The image of a foot slipping would have been felt physically by people who walked wadis after rain, where wet rock gives way without warning under someone who was sure of his step.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the argument as having no footing occurs only in this ayah. Related forms of its root appear three times elsewhere, twice for false argument aimed at knocking the truth off its feet and once for a man who lost a drawing of lots. The root's ordinary sense is a foot sliding on smooth ground.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage evaluates an argument by its footing rather than its content, which is a claim about the arguer's position and not about logic. Someone disputing after they have seen the matter answered is doing something different from someone honestly unconvinced, and the Quran treats the two very differently elsewhere. The severity here belongs to the first case, and it is worth noticing how narrowly the ayah draws it.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who dispute about God's signs without any warrant, and names pride as what is really moving them.
Says disbelievers argue with falsehood to drive back the truth, using a related form of the same root.
Pictures a person disputing about God with no knowledge, no guidance and no illuminating book.

studies.applyIt: Think of a position you defend that you first took for reasons you no longer use. Say the current reasons out loud and hear whether they hold. You are not obliged to change anything. But this ayah is about arguing from a place your own feet left some time ago, and that is worth checking once.

studies.title: I Ask Of You No Wage
studies.meaning: The messenger states that he asks no payment, and then names an exception, and it is the exception the commentators record several readings of. Some take it as affection within kinship generally, so that what is asked is that people keep their family ties. Some take it as affection toward the near relatives of the one bringing the message. Some read it as drawing near to God through good work. The classical sources set the range out without collapsing it. The clause that follows is not disputed at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Refusing a wage is something the Quran's prophets say repeatedly, each to his own people, and the objection it answers was live in Mecca, where any new public voice was assumed to be speaking for a paymaster. The surah has just described people who want the harvest of this world. Commentators differ over this ayah's placement, some treating it as Medinan inside a Meccan surah, and they do not settle it.

keyTerms.note: Connected to the word for skin, because news shows in a face before it is spoken. The verb names the delivery of good news specifically, and its opposite is used for warning.
An abstract noun for closeness that the Quran uses for relatives. Because it names the relation rather than the people, the phrase built on it can be read in more than one direction.
Usually used of acquiring a wrong, from a root meaning to scrape together. Applying it to a good deed is deliberate, and it keeps the sense of something gathered by effort rather than received.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man who spoke publicly in Arabia was assumed to be speaking for someone: a patron, a clan, or his own advancement. Poets were commissioned. Soothsayers charged fees. The first question asked about any new voice was who was funding it and what they wanted. In that setting a public refusal of payment was not a pious flourish but a claim anyone could test over time.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence about asking no wage is repeated, in almost identical words, by five different prophets within a single surah of the Quran. Noah, then Hud, Salih, Lot and Shu'ayb each say it to their own people in turn, so the refusal of payment is presented as a recurring mark of the office rather than a personal choice.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The clause everyone agrees on is the one about increase, and it describes something more than a larger payment: the goodness of the deed itself is enlarged. The refusal of a wage matters in a different way. It removes the one motive that would make the message a transaction, and it is placed in the messenger's own mouth rather than asserted about him by someone else.

crossReferences.why: Gives the first of the five identical refusals in that surah, spoken by Noah to his own people.
Repeats the refusal and names what the message is instead: a reminder for all the worlds.
States the increase this ayah promises, a good deed multiplied and no one wronged by an atom's weight.

studies.applyIt: Contact one relative you have not spoken to in a year and have nothing to ask them. No news to deliver, no favour, no occasion. Five minutes. Every reading the commentators give of this ayah has affection and nearness in it somewhere, and the version nearest to hand is usually the one that has been left longest.

studies.title: And He Pardons Much
studies.meaning: A hard sentence followed by a clause that is easy to read past: whatever strikes you comes of what your hands earned, and He pardons much. The commentators place real weight on the second half, several noting that without it the first would describe a world of exact settlement in which every difficulty could be read backwards as a verdict. The word for pardoning means effacing, wiping a mark off a surface. Then the passage moves to ships standing in the sea like landmarks, held up by nothing the passengers arranged.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayat just before describe provision measured out precisely, because unlimited provision would produce excess, and rain sent down after people have given up expecting it. The surah is arguing that what looks like restriction is calibration. This passage extends the argument to misfortune, and the ships lead directly into a warning two lines later that the wind could simply be stilled.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to hit a target. The word treats a misfortune as something aimed and landing rather than as an accident, which is why the sentence can then ask where it came from.
The root means to wipe out a trace, and was used of wind erasing tracks in sand. Pardon in Arabic is therefore a mark removed rather than a penalty waived on a record that stands.
The plural covers both a raised marker and a mountain, and travellers navigated by such things. Ships are described by the one thing on a flat horizon that tells you where you are.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Both images came from navigation. Wind effaced tracks in sand within hours, which is why the word for pardoning was a picture from the desert rather than from a court or a ledger. And a ship on the Red Sea rose above a flat horizon so that it could be seen from a long way off, standing where the raised stones stood that guided caravans across country without a road.
studies.didYouKnow: The three-word clause about pardoning much occurs twice within five ayat here. It appears in this passage attached to misfortune, and again a few lines later attached to the same ships, which are said to be wreckable for what their passengers have earned, and then are not. The same phrase closes two different arguments in one stretch of text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage affirms a connection between conduct and consequence and refuses an exact accounting in this life, which are usually offered as alternatives. Because much is pardoned, nobody can read their circumstances backwards into a verdict about themselves or anyone else. The ships then make the same point structurally: what is holding you up is not the thing you assumed was holding you up.

crossReferences.why: States the consequence of exact settlement, that nothing living would be left on the surface of the earth.
Draws the same connection between what hands earn and what surfaces in the world, with a stated purpose.
Repeats the pardon clause a few lines later, applied to the same ships and what could happen to them.

studies.applyIt: Take one difficulty you are currently in and refuse, for today only, both of the explanations you usually reach for: that you brought it on yourself, and that it is arbitrary. Sit with it unexplained for a day. This passage puts a large clause of pardon between the cause and the effect, and that clause is precisely what makes the reading impossible.

studies.title: Whoever Pardons And Puts Right
studies.meaning: Two things are set out in one sentence and the order is deliberate. First a ceiling: the repayment of a wrong is a wrong equal to it, which caps redress at equivalence and closes off escalation. Then an alternative that is offered rather than required, and it has two parts. Whoever pardons and puts things right has his reward with God. The commentators notice that the second verb is not forgoing but repairing, so what is described is reconstruction rather than silence. The closing clause explains why the ceiling exists.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The ayah sits inside a run describing the community's own qualities: they answer their Lord, keep the prayer, decide their affairs by consultation among themselves, spend from what they are given, forgive when angry, and defend themselves when wronged. This line stands between the last two and holds both of them. The surah takes its name from a single word in that list.

keyTerms.note: A return that corresponds to what preceded it, used equally of reward and of penalty. The word already contains the idea of proportion, which the phrase after it then states explicitly.
Exact equivalence, not an approximation. Placing it immediately after the word for recompense sets a ceiling rather than a floor, which is the reverse of how feuds actually worked.
From the root of soundness and repair, used of mending a thing that has broken. Joined to pardon, it describes rebuilding a relation rather than merely declining to press a claim.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Vengeance in Arabia rarely stayed level. A killing was answered by killing someone of greater standing, and feuds ran for generations because each side settled at a premium and the other then owed the difference. Poets recorded and inflamed them, naming the dead in verse that travelled. In that setting a limit of exact equivalence was not leniency. It was the first thing capable of stopping a cycle.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah takes its name from one word inside the list of qualities just above this ayah, describing a community that settles its affairs by mutual consultation. The name comes from a method rather than from a doctrine, a narrative or an opening letter, which makes it unusual among the surah names in use.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A ceiling is set and then a door is opened above it. Equivalence is named as the limit of what redress may reach, and pardon joined to repair is placed in a different economy, with the reward held by God rather than paid by the person who did the wrong. The final clause does quiet work on the injured party, since going past the measure would move them across the line it draws.

crossReferences.why: States the same equivalence and then adds that patience would be better for those who are patient.
Presses pardon by an argument from self-interest: would you not love that God should forgive you?
Places patience joined to forgiveness among the matters of firm resolve, three ayat later.

studies.applyIt: Take a grievance you are genuinely entitled to press. Then ask what putting it right would actually involve, as distinct from being owed for it: a conversation, a thing replaced, a relation resumed. Write the two answers separately. This ayah names two verbs, and most of us do only the first one and call it the second.

studies.title: No Blame On Those Wronged
studies.meaning: Three short ayat holding two things at once. Someone who takes redress after being wronged has no case standing against them, and the case lies instead with those who wrong people and overreach in the land. Then the last line moves, without contradicting either, to the other option: whoever is patient and forgives, that belongs to the firm resolve of matters. The commentators read the balance carefully. The right to answer is protected in the first two ayat precisely so that the forgiveness in the third can be a choice.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The passage closes a section describing the community's own qualities, and the sequence is unusual: self-defence, then a limit of exact equivalence, then pardon, then the right to redress again, then patience. That layering suggests an audience under real pressure and needing both permissions at once, which fits the situation in Mecca, where believers were being harmed and had little power to answer anything.

keyTerms.note: From the root of help and victory, in a form meaning to obtain that for oneself. It covers seeking justice as well as striking back, and the Arabic does not separate the two here.
Literally a road. The idiom means a route by which someone can be reached with a claim, so denying a way against a person is denying anyone standing to bring one.
Settled intention that has hardened into commitment. The phrase built on it names the things that require it, and the Quran uses the same phrase in only a few places.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Standing was defended publicly or lost publicly. A man who did not answer a wrong lost the presumption that his household was protected, and others adjusted their behaviour toward him within days. Redress in that world was not personal satisfaction; it was the mechanism by which a family remained safe to live among neighbours. That makes the third of these ayat expensive in a way a modern reader can easily miss.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase in the last ayah for what belongs to firm resolve appears in only a few places in the Quran. One of them is a father's counsel to his son, where it closes a list of prayer, calling to what is right, forbidding wrong and patience under what befalls you. The same words mark two very different things at the top of the same scale.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two positions usually treated as alternatives are held together. A wronged person's right to answer is protected, and stepping past it is described as strength rather than as weakness or as loss. The ordering carries the argument: forgiveness is presented as an act available to someone who had the option and did not need it, which is a different thing entirely from the resignation of someone who never had one.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase for firm resolve, closing a father's list of what to hold to under pressure.
Attaches the same phrase to patience under abuse from others, in a passage about being tested.
Sets the ceiling this passage assumes, redress capped at exact equivalence with pardon above it.

studies.applyIt: Think of one wrong you could still answer and have not. Decide in actual words which of the two you are doing: choosing to let it go, or lacking the means to act. Both are honest positions. Only one of them is what this passage calls resolve, and the difference is invisible from outside and obvious from inside.
